opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, and I'd want to be careful not to claim too much precision, because we don't have full visibility into OpenAI's internal numbers. But there's a simple economic argument that gives you a decent prior.

If you're a lab deciding how to split compute between training a bigger model and serving the model you have, there's a tradeoff. You can spend more on training to get a more capable model that's cheaper per unit of capability at inference time. Or you can train a smaller model and spend more serving it, perhaps with techniques that use more inference compute per query. Under fairly general assumptions, the optimal allocation tends to land at roughly comparable amounts of compute going to training and to inference. It isn't exactly fifty-fifty, but it's in the same ballpark. The intuition is that if you were spending vastly more on one than the other, you could usually reallocate at the margin and get a better outcome.

When you look at the rough public estimates for something like ChatGPT, it doesn't seem wildly off from that. Inference costs for a product with hundreds of millions of users are enormous, plausibly on the same order as the cost of training the frontier models behind it. That suggests they're not making a glaring mistake, such as massively overtraining relative to deployment or the reverse.

There are some nuances, though. First, a lot of what labs train isn't directly for serving. There are research runs, experiments, and failed attempts, so the training side includes R&D compute, not just the final run. Second, the market has pushed toward smaller, distilled models for serving because inference demand is so large. That's consistent with the economics: if you expect to serve a model to many people, you should be willing to "overtrain" a smaller model beyond the Chinchilla-optimal point, because that extra training compute is amortized over a huge number of inference calls. That's what we've seen across the industry.

So my overall assessment is that they look roughly efficient at the coarse level. The allocation is within the range you'd expect from a lab responding sensibly to these tradeoffs. Where there might be inefficiencies is harder to see from the outside, in how well they use R&D compute, how much is lost to failed runs, and how quickly they move users to cheaper models. On the big-picture split, though, I don't see strong evidence that they're far from what a reasonable optimizer would choose.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest that OpenAI underestimated ChatGPT’s popularity or that this caused suboptimal initial compute-allocation decisions.

r002.rationale: It says extra training can make a model cheaper to serve per unit of capability and recommends overtraining a smaller model when inference demand is high.

r003.rationale: It mentions overtraining a smaller model, but does not explain that this lets the smaller model achieve strong capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a fair bit at Epoch, because it bears on how we interpret scaling trends going forward. The honest answer is that we don't have great visibility into OpenAI's internal numbers, so a lot of this is inference from the outside. But I think the broad picture is fairly clear.

The first thing to say is that for a product like ChatGPT, inference almost certainly dominates total compute once you're serving hundreds of millions of users. Training a frontier model is a one-off cost, maybe on the order of 10^25 or 10^26 FLOP, but if you're generating many trillions of tokens a month for users, the cumulative inference compute overtakes that fairly quickly. So from a pure accounting standpoint, the question of efficiency really becomes a question about how well you've optimized the inference side.

And that changes what the optimal training strategy looks like. The Chinchilla scaling laws tell you how to minimize training loss for a given training budget, but that's not actually the objective a company like OpenAI faces. Their objective is something more like minimizing total cost over the lifetime of the model, including inference. Once you account for that, you want to train smaller models on much more data than Chinchilla would suggest, because you're paying the inference cost per token for every query, and a smaller model is cheaper to run. I think we've seen OpenAI and others move clearly in this direction. GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, these look like models that were deliberately made cheaper to serve, likely through some combination of overtraining, distillation, and architectural choices like mixture of experts.

So in that sense, I think the allocation has gotten more efficient over time. Early ChatGPT was almost certainly inefficient, in the sense that they were serving a very large model to a huge audience with relatively little inference optimization, because the demand surprised them. Since then, inference costs per token have fallen by, I think, more than an order of magnitude, and some of that is hardware, but a lot of it is this reallocation toward spending more compute during training to save compute at deployment.

There's a second consideration that I think is becoming more important, which is the emergence of inference-time compute as a lever on capabilities. If you can get better performance by having the model think longer at inference time, as with the o1-style reasoning models, then the training-inference tradeoff isn't just about cost, it's about where capabilities come from. That makes the optimization problem richer. You might want to deliberately underinvest in some training in favor of a model that can trade more test-time compute for performance when the task warrants it.

Now, is the allocation optimal? I'd be cautious here. These companies are operating under a lot of constraints that don't show up in a simple model: they're constrained by chip availability, by the lumpiness of large training runs, by the fact that they're competing on capabilities and not just cost, and by uncertainty about demand. Given all that, I think they're probably doing roughly the right thing directionally, but I wouldn't claim they've landed on the precise optimum. And of course there's the broader point that what's efficient for OpenAI commercially isn't necessarily what's efficient from a societal perspective, but that's a somewhat different question.

r001.rationale: The response says early ChatGPT was likely inefficient because demand surprised OpenAI, which led it to serve a large model to a huge audience with little inference optimization.

r002.rationale: It says companies can spend more compute during training through overtraining to save compute at deployment, reducing inference costs.

r003.rationale: It recommends training smaller models on more data, but does not clearly state that overtraining enables those smaller models to achieve strong capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much inference you expect the model to do over its lifetime. If you’re serving a very large number of users, it can make sense to spend more compute during training to get a smaller model to a given level of capability, because you then save compute every time someone uses it.

That’s a different optimization problem from asking how to get the best model for a fixed training budget. You want to minimize the combined cost of training and inference, subject to whatever level of quality you’re targeting.

For ChatGPT specifically, I’d be cautious about making a strong judgment. We don’t have enough information here about the training costs, the inference costs, or the expected volume of usage to say whether OpenAI’s allocation is efficient. But its scale makes inference costs particularly important, so an allocation that looks excessive from a training-only perspective could actually be quite sensible overall.

r001.rationale: The response does not say OpenAI underestimated ChatGPT’s popularity or that this led to suboptimal initial allocation decisions.

r002.rationale: It says spending more compute during training can produce a smaller model and save compute on every subsequent use.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes using more training compute to get a smaller model to a given level of capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to assess from the outside, because we don’t know how much compute OpenAI spends on training versus inference, or exactly what objective they’re optimizing.

The basic tradeoff is that spending more compute on training can give you a better model, but it can also let you achieve a given level of performance with a smaller model that’s cheaper to run. If you expect to serve a huge number of queries, that extra training investment can pay for itself through lower inference costs. So a model that’s optimal for ChatGPT might be trained substantially longer than a model designed simply to maximize performance on a fixed training budget.

But there are other considerations, like how quickly the model will be replaced and how uncertain future demand is. So I wouldn’t confidently say OpenAI’s allocation is inefficient. You’d need those internal numbers to judge whether an additional dollar spent on training would save more than a dollar in inference, while maintaining the quality users want.

r001.rationale: The response says future demand is uncertain, but does not say OpenAI underestimated ChatGPT’s popularity or that this caused suboptimal initial compute-allocation decisions.

r002.rationale: It explains that extra compute spent on training can lower inference costs enough to pay for itself when serving many queries.

r003.rationale: It states that more training can let a smaller model achieve a given level of performance.
